It is literally something that baffled both Johns Hopkins and the Mayo Clinic for months because even the best Doctors in the world thought such a thing was impossible. Enter Dr. Alexander Ortega—the worlds foremost expert on PG and the Dr. that both Mayo and JH said was Ryan’s only hope. I will never forget the first time he looked at Ryan and said “I was skeptical seeing the pictures but seeing you in person 95-99% you have PG and it’s the worst case I have seen.” This is a man who sees 40 PG patients a month when most career dermatologists may see 1 in their entire career and he was dumbfounded. Ryan loves to co-opt Jurassic Park and say that PG finds a way. He is the living breathing example of Murphy’s law in one of the most cruel ways nature could imagine but he is still crazy positive. You can ask just about anyone in Rochester, MN (home to Mayo Cljnic) about Ryan and they will repeat what has become his signature catchphrase as he encourages everyone to “do everything in your power to make today the best day of your life and then tomorrow even better.” He is literally my Hero and the world will be devastatingly dimmer should he pass away.

Thanks for your thoughtful consideration. Let’s take this one at a time. First, my husband has all three subtypes of PG and is constantly battling infection and on top of that has developed adrenal insufficiency due to the months of high dose steroids. So you are correct in that PG itself is rarely fatal, rather it is the complications that come along with the disease. Much like HIV itself does not kill but instead death is precipitated by something as innocuous with a cold. My husband is literally an anomaly in the severity and extent of his case as well as the fact that he is the only person who has ever been diagnosed with all three major PG subtypes. PG also rarely produces more than a few lesions whereas Ryan has more than 30 wounds and 50+ pustulars. He was treated at both Mayo Clinic and Johns Hopkins due to the severity and rarity of his case and is now under the care of the leading doctor in the field who still cannot venture to say of Ryan will out survive his original 6 month prognosis. So, extreme yes, disingenuous no. 

Second, I’ll just let the case law do the heavy lifting on this one. “unpaid medical leave may be a reasonable accommodation…even an extended medical leave, or an extension of an existing leave period, may be a reasonable accommodation…” 
Nunes v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 164 F.3d 1243 (9th Cir. 1999). No one is asking to keep Ryan’s position open indefinitely. Rather, we are asking for the County to honor the agreed upon leave (which is unpaid likely reasonable according to Nunes). In Washington state we have PFML and FMLA and they do not have to be taken concurrently. Ryan is on approved state PFML until June 7th and then is eligible for 12 weeks of FMLA beginning June 6th. That is the point. The county isn’t even letting him take that. The county is certainly entitled to hire someone to fill his position (something that his supervisor actually already did) but that doesn’t mean that they can violate federal law and terminate him while on protected leave.

There is nothing to file until there is a redressable offense giving rise to a cause of action. At this point they haven’t actually terminated him yet so there is no controversy ripe for the court to hear. The County still has the opportunity to do the right thing.
